subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.section_ref: Let's Take a Look Around Us!
periods.textbook_anchor: Let's Take a Look Around Us! — Draw a picture of your classroom and label the things drawn (p. 124)

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites students to look slowly around the classroom — walls, floor, ceiling, furniture, windows — and share aloud what they notice. Students name objects one by one while the teacher writes a few on the board to spark ideas.

Students open Textbook p. 124 and follow the drawing activity: each child draws their classroom in their notebook and labels every object they include. Encourage detail — window frames, shelves, hooks, mats — and accepting any legible label spelling.
Students share their drawings in pairs, pointing out objects the partner may have missed. The class makes a combined spoken list of all the different objects named across the room.

Quick closing round: the teacher asks 'Look at two things in your drawing — can you guess what they are made of?' Students say one or two guesses aloud. No answers confirmed yet — curiosity stays open.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe their immediate environment and record what they find through labelled drawing.
periods.section_context: Classroom objects drawn and labelled by students; Khushi's classroom drawing scenario.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Did anyone draw something their neighbour did not? What is it made of — do you know?' This surfaces the material-identification thread naturally and invites students to notice variety without pressure.

periods.activity_title: Testing What We Can See Through
periods.textbook_anchor: See-through Materials! — Look at a light bulb or candle flame through collected objects and order them from most to least see-through (p. 126)
materials: a candle or torch as light source
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure showing transparent, translucent, and opaque examples (p. 126)

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds up a glass and asks students whether they can see through it. Then holds up a thick book — can they? Students predict verbally. The teacher introduces the idea that materials differ in how much light passes through them, referencing the scenario of Khushi seeing a tree through a windowpane (Textbook p. 126).

In small groups, students collect the provided objects and take turns holding each one up between their eyes and the candle or torch. They arrange the objects in a line from most see-through to least see-through and then record their order in their notebooks with a brief word about each (e.g., 'clear', 'blurry', 'nothing').

Groups share their ordered lines. The teacher introduces the three words — transparent, translucent, opaque — and maps them to the groups' own ordering using the textbook figure. Students write the three terms and one example each in their notebooks.
Closing question: the teacher asks students to look around the classroom and silently point to one transparent thing, one opaque thing. A few students share and the class confirms.

periods.implied_lo: Students can sort materials by an observable physical property using a systematic hands-on test.
periods.section_context: Plastic bottles, paper, cloth, candle or torch light source; transparent, translucent, opaque classification.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why might a window be made of glass and not cloth or paper?' This anchors the property to everyday design decisions and invites students to connect material choice to purpose.

periods.textbook_anchor: See-through Materials! — Look at white paper through coloured transparent bags or bottles and observe whether colour appears to change (p. 127)
materials: coloured transparent plastic bags or bottles (blue, yellow, red, green — at least two colours per group)
sheet of white paper per group

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds a white sheet and asks: 'What colour is this paper?' Students agree — white. Then the teacher holds a coloured transparent bag in front of it and asks again. Students observe and respond. The class is curious about why the colour seems to change.

Students open Textbook p. 127 and carry out the activity: they look at a white sheet through each coloured transparent object in turn, then look at a coloured object through a different coloured transparent material. They record their observations in a simple table in their notebooks — columns for 'material used', 'colour seen through it', and 'surprise or not?'.

Students share what surprised them most. The teacher guides a brief discussion: when have they seen coloured glass or plastic in real life — coloured spectacles, festival decorations, coloured water bottles? Students recall and connect.
Students write one sentence in their notebooks: 'I noticed that when I looked through ______ colour, the white paper looked ______.' Teacher circulates and reads a few aloud.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record how a material's colour property affects what is seen through it.
periods.section_context: Coloured transparent plastic bags and bottles in blue, yellow, red, green; white paper; coloured objects viewed through different coloured transparent materials.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Have you ever worn or seen tinted glasses or sunglasses? What do things look like through them?' Connecting to familiar personal experience makes the optical observation concrete and memorable.

periods.textbook_anchor: What is it made of? — Complete Khushi's materials table and add a new row for a material not in her list (p. 128)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook table of materials and objects (p. 128)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud a few of the materials in Khushi's table (Textbook p. 128) — wood, metal, glass, plastic — and asks: 'Where does wood come from? Where does metal come from?' Students discuss in pairs for a moment, then share. The teacher traces each material briefly back to its natural source on the board.

Students complete the third column of Khushi's table (Textbook p. 128) by writing names of objects they have seen made of each material. They then add at least one new row for a material not in the table — clay or rubber are suggested in the textbook, but students may choose another they know from home.

A whole-class 'chain game': the teacher points to one student who names a material, the next names an object made of it, the next names where that material comes from in nature, and the next adds whether they have that object at home. The chain travels around the room briskly.

The teacher poses the reflection questions from Textbook p. 129: 'Ask an elder at home — was your spoon always made of this material? Have materials changed over time?' Students note the question to ask at home (no prior homework required — this is a fresh prompt).

periods.implied_lo: Students can group everyday objects by the material they are made of and trace that material to a natural source.
periods.section_context: Wood, metal, glass, plastic, clay, rubber; Khushi's materials table; natural sources of materials (trees, ore, sand); spoon material inquiry.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does anyone have something at home made of clay or cane that your grandparent uses but you do not?' This draws out intergenerational material knowledge without labelling it — students from different backgrounds will contribute different traditional objects.

periods.activity_title: Odd Pairs — Wrong Material, Right Reason
periods.textbook_anchor: Does it Bend? — List five objects paired with an unsuitable material and explain why those materials will not work (p. 130)
materials: small pieces of wood (e.g., a ruler or wooden block)
a strip of metal (metal ruler or spoon handle)
a piece of glass or thick glass bangle (handled safely)

time_bands.activity: The teacher taps the metal spoon gently on the wooden object, then the plastic piece, then the cloth. Students listen and describe the sounds in their own words. The teacher asks: 'Why does each sound differently? What does that tell us about the material?' Students discuss the idea that materials feel and behave differently — hard, soft, flexible, rigid.

The teacher poses the textbook question (p. 130): 'Could we make a table out of cloth? Could we make a raincoat out of wood?' Students respond with laughter and reasons. The teacher names the key idea: hardness and flexibility determine whether a material suits a purpose.

Students open Textbook p. 130 and write their own 'Odd Pairs' — five objects each paired with a material that would NOT work for making it, and a reason why. Pairs discuss before writing to check each other's reasoning.

Students share their most surprising or funny odd pair aloud. The class evaluates: does the reason make sense? The teacher invites students to think of one real example from home where a material was chosen because it is hard, or because it is flexible.
Brief close: students complete the sentence 'A ______ must be made of ______ because ______.' in their notebooks.

periods.implied_lo: Students can match a material to a use-requirement (hardness or flexibility) and explain why an unsuitable material would fail.
periods.section_context: Wood, metal, plastic, cloth, glass; metal spoon tapping activity; hardness and flexibility as material properties; Odd Pairs writing task.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What would happen to a cloth chair after one person sat on it? Would it still work the next day?' Probing the consequence of a wrong material choice deepens reasoning beyond simple recall.

periods.activity_title: Solid, Liquid, or Gas — Sorting Matter
periods.textbook_anchor: Does it Flow? — Sort given objects (ink, stone, smoke, ice, steam, spoon, honey, bottle, bag, water) into solid, liquid, and gas, and identify confusing cases like sand, sponge, and clay (p. 132)
materials: small container of honey or oil (optional, to observe flow)
a handful of dry sand in a container (optional)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of tray, bottle, and balloon representing solid, liquid, and gas (p. 132)

time_bands.activity: The teacher places a stone and a cup of water on the desk. 'Does the stone change shape if I put it in the cup? Does the water?' Students observe and answer. The teacher introduces the three categories — solid, liquid, gas — with one quick example each (stone, water, air), linking to the textbook's tray-bottle-balloon diagram (Textbook p. 132).

Students open Textbook p. 132 and sort the listed objects — ink, a stone, smoke, ice, steam, a spoon, honey, a bottle, a bag, water — into the three categories, writing each name in the appropriate symbol (tray for solid, bottle for liquid, balloon for gas) in their notebooks. They add at least two of their own examples to each category.

The teacher draws attention to the confusing cases: sand, sponge, clay. Students discuss in small groups — 'Is sand a solid or a liquid? Why might it be confusing?' Groups share their reasoning. The teacher confirms that small solid pieces can look like they flow but each grain is still a solid.
Closing: each student writes one sentence naming one confusing case and explaining which state it really belongs to and why.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify matter into solid, liquid, and gas based on observable properties of shape and flow.
periods.section_context: Ink, stone, smoke, ice, steam, spoon, honey, bottle, bag, water; sand, sponge, clay as edge cases; tray-bottle-balloon sorting framework.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Where does air go when you open a bag of air outside? Where does water go when you pour it on the floor?' These simple prompts ground the gas and liquid definitions in students' lived experience without requiring laboratory equipment.

periods.activity_title: Natural or Artificial — Sorting and Drawing
periods.textbook_anchor: Natural — Artificial — List five things in each group: Natural and Artificial (p. 133)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of Khushi's mango tree drawing (p. 133)

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a quick mango tree on the board and asks: 'Did anyone make this tree? Or did it grow on its own?' Students respond. Then the teacher draws a chair: 'Did anyone make this? Or did it grow?' Students see the distinction. The teacher introduces the terms natural and artificial, referencing Khushi's mango tree illustration (Textbook p. 133).

Students open Textbook p. 133 and complete the Write task — listing five natural things and five artificial things. The teacher encourages variety: can they include things from outside the classroom? From their home? From nature around the school?

Students draw three natural things and three artificial things in their notebooks (a gentle preview of the reflection task to follow). Encourage detail and colour. Students who finish early add labels naming the material each natural thing is made of or where it comes from.

Discussion: the teacher holds up the mango tree question from Textbook p. 133 — 'At what time of year did Khushi draw her picture — around January or around June?' Students reason from when mangoes ripen in their own experience or region, and share their guess with a reason.

periods.implied_lo: Students can distinguish natural from artificial things in their environment and represent that distinction through labelled drawing.
periods.section_context: Mango tree; natural things (plants, animals, rocks, water, air); artificial things (clothes, shoes, tables); seasonal reasoning about mango ripening; five-item lists for each category.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Is a pot made of clay natural or artificial? What about a clay brick?' This edge case — natural material, human-shaped form — prompts richer thinking about the boundary between natural and artificial.

periods.activity_title: Reflect, Match, and Share — Chapter Consolidation
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Match transparent, translucent, and opaque to a lamp shade made of paper, a plate, and a glass used in spectacles (p. 134)
materials: a shining spoon (metal or painted — one or two to pass around)

time_bands.activity: The teacher passes around a shining spoon and asks: 'Is it metal, or is it another material painted to look shiny? How would you find out without being told?' Students suggest tests — tapping it, bending it slightly, feeling how cold it is, checking if it is heavy. The class discusses which test is most useful, drawing on the material properties explored earlier in the chapter.

Students open Textbook p. 134 and complete the Write task (three common materials) and the Discuss task (the shining spoon investigation) in their notebooks independently, then compare answers with a partner.

Students complete the matching activity (Textbook p. 134): they draw lines connecting transparent, translucent, and opaque to a lamp shade made of paper, a plate, and a glass used in spectacles, writing a brief reason for each match.

Whole-class discussion: the teacher reads each match and asks a student to justify it in their own words. Other students agree or respectfully challenge. The teacher affirms the reasoning process, not just the answer.
Closing: each student writes one thing from this chapter that they found surprising or that they want to tell someone at home. Two or three students share aloud.

periods.implied_lo: Students can apply material property vocabulary to identify and justify the classification of familiar objects.
periods.section_context: Shining spoon (metal vs. painted material); three common materials naming; transparent, translucent, opaque matched to lamp shade of paper, plate, spectacle glass; three natural and three artificial things.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you had to teach a younger child what transparent means, what example would you use — not the ones in the book?' This pushes students beyond recall into genuine understanding and gives the teacher a quick window into who has internalised the concept.

assessment_items.task: Draw your classroom in your notebook. Label at least six things in your drawing. Next to each label, write what material that thing is made of — for example, 'door — wood' or 'window — glass'.
assessment_items.scaffold: Step 1: Look slowly around the classroom. Step 2: Draw the room as you see it — walls, floor, furniture, door, windows. Step 3: Write the name of each thing you drew. Step 4: Write the material next to each name. If you are not sure, make your best guess.
assessment_items.annotation: A complete response names at least six objects and provides a material for each. Accept any reasonable material name — 'iron' for metal parts, 'wood' for wooden parts, 'cement' for walls. Look for the student's willingness to look carefully and connect an object to its source material, not perfect spelling.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Let's Take a Look Around Us!
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe their immediate environment and record what they find through labelled drawing.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can look at their familiar environment with a material-aware eye and use drawing and labelling as a record-keeping tool — the core skill of observation and creative presentation combined.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The four-step scaffold guides students who freeze at a blank page; students who are confident may skip directly to drawing. The key check is whether labels name the material, not just the object.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: six or more objects labelled with specific, plausible materials and a drawing that shows spatial thinking. Weak: objects named but materials left blank, or all materials written as 'material' without specifics.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may describe their classroom in a numbered list with materials. Students who know very few English material names may write in their home language — the teacher can note the word for the record.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing and labelling is the exact mode this section's activity uses; it is also a low-language-barrier route that lets all students participate regardless of writing fluency.

assessment_items.question_text: Mira holds a thick piece of cloth up to a candle flame. She cannot see the flame at all through the cloth. What best describes the cloth?
assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: C. The cloth blocks all light, so it is opaque. This item directly tests the outcome of the hands-on sorting activity.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can sort materials by an observable physical property using a systematic hands-on test.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'Transparent' indicates the student has reversed the concept — transparent means you can see through clearly, which is the opposite of what is described.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'Translucent' suggests partial understanding — the student knows the word is in the same family but has not distinguished between partial and zero light transmission.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'Flexible' shows the student has confused a different material property (flexibility from the 'Does it Bend?' section) with light-transmission properties.

assessment_items.question_text: Ramu looks at a white sheet of paper through a thin blue plastic bag. He then looks at the same sheet through a thin yellow plastic bag. Describe what Ramu is likely to observe in each case and explain why the colour appears to change.
expected_elements: The white paper appears blue (or bluish) when viewed through the blue plastic bag.
The white paper appears yellow (or yellowish) when viewed through the yellow plastic bag.
The colour appears to change because the coloured transparent material lets through only its own colour of light (or adds its colour to what you see).
assessment_items.annotation: A full response names the observed colour in each case and offers a reason connected to the material's colour. Accept informal language ('the bag puts its colour on the paper'). Deduct if only one case is answered or no reason is given.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record how a material's colour property affects what is seen through it.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: The white paper appears blue (or bluish) when viewed through the blue plastic bag.
The white paper appears yellow (or yellowish) when viewed through the yellow plastic bag.
The colour appears to change because the coloured transparent material lets through only its own colour of light (or adds its colour to what you see).

assessment_items.question_text: Priya wants to add a new row to a materials table. She chooses clay. Write one object made of clay and trace clay back to where it comes from in nature.
expected_elements: A named object made of clay (e.g., pot, clay lamp, kulhad, tile, brick).
Clay comes from the Earth / soil / the ground (a natural source is named).
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any correct clay object — regional examples such as kulhad, terracotta pot, clay idol, or tile are all valid. The natural-source answer should reference earth, soil, or the ground. Regional variation in clay objects is expected and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can group everyday objects by the material they are made of and trace that material to a natural source.

competency.competency_text: Describes usage of natural resources in their immediate environment

expected_elements: A named object made of clay (e.g., pot, clay lamp, kulhad, tile, brick).
Clay comes from the Earth / soil / the ground (a natural source is named).

assessment_items.question_text: Arnav wants to make a water bucket out of cloth. Write two reasons why cloth would not be a good material for a bucket.
expected_elements: Cloth is not hard or rigid — it will not hold its shape, so the bucket would collapse.
Cloth lets water pass through (or absorb it) — the water would leak out and the bucket would not hold water.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for two distinct reasons, each connected to a material property (hardness/rigidity or water-absorption/flexibility). Partial credit for one correct reason. Accept informal phrasing — 'the cloth will fall down' is acceptable if it conveys lack of rigidity.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can match a material to a use-requirement (hardness or flexibility) and explain why an unsuitable material would fail.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with disciplinary core ideas in the natural sciences, as well as in engineering, technology, and applications of science, which reflect the content that will be learned across subject areas in later Grades

expected_elements: Cloth is not hard or rigid — it will not hold its shape, so the bucket would collapse.
Cloth lets water pass through (or absorb it) — the water would leak out and the bucket would not hold water.

assessment_items.question_text: Sand looks like it can pour and flow like a liquid. Why is sand still classified as a solid?

options.label: A
options.text: Because each grain of sand keeps its own shape and does not change shape on its own.

options.label: B
options.text: Because sand is dry and liquids are always wet.

options.label: C
options.text: Because sand is found in nature and liquids are made by people.

options.label: D
options.text: Because sand is heavy and liquids are light.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. This item directly targets the edge-case discussion about sand from the sorting activity. The correct answer captures the defining property of a solid — each particle retains its shape.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify matter into solid, liquid, and gas based on observable properties of shape and flow.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option shows the student is using a surface property (dryness vs. wetness) rather than the defining scientific criterion of shape retention — a common sensory misconception.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option reveals confusion between the natural-vs-artificial classification and the solid-liquid-gas classification — two different frameworks introduced in the same chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student is using mass or weight as the criterion rather than shape — a common alternative conception about why things behave differently.

assessment_items.task: Draw three natural things and three artificial things in your notebook. Label each drawing. Below each natural thing, write one word that tells where it comes from (for example: 'grows', 'found in earth', 'found in sky'). Below each artificial thing, write who or what makes it (for example: 'made by people', 'made in a factory').
assessment_items.scaffold: Step 1: Think of three things that exist in nature without people making them — draw these. Step 2: Think of three things that people make or build — draw these. Step 3: Write a label (name) on each drawing. Step 4: Add a short note below each: where does the natural thing come from? Who makes the artificial thing?
format_of_output: six labelled drawings (three natural, three artificial)
a short note below each drawing about origin or maker
assessment_items.annotation: A complete response includes three clearly natural items (plants, animals, rocks, rivers, clouds, etc.) and three clearly artificial items (furniture, clothes, vehicles, tools, etc.), each labelled and accompanied by an origin note. Accept any valid examples — regional flora, local animals, and traditional crafted objects are all correct. Regional variation in examples is expected and welcome.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can distinguish natural from artificial things in their environment and represent that distinction through labelled drawing.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can apply the natural-versus-artificial distinction to self-chosen examples and use drawing and brief annotation to present that understanding — showing both conceptual grasp and observational range.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold breaks the task into choosing, drawing, labelling, and annotating — four separate acts. Students who already understand the concept may move through quickly; the scaffold is a safety net, not a ceiling.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: six distinct drawings across both categories, labels that show variety (not all trees, not all chairs), and origin notes that use the right language ('grows in soil', 'made in a factory'). Weak: fewer than six drawings, both categories from the same narrow domain (e.g., all furniture, all trees), or origin notes left blank.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may substitute a labelled list with a brief description of each item. Students who know an object in their home language may write the home-language name with an English translation attempt beside it.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing is the mode explicitly called for in the textbook's Let us reflect task; paired annotation shifts the task from copying examples to demonstrating understanding of the category distinction.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at these three objects: (i) a lamp shade made of paper, (ii) a glass used in spectacles, (iii) a ceramic plate. Which option correctly matches each object to transparent, translucent, or opaque?

options.label: A
options.text: Lamp shade — opaque; spectacle glass — transparent; plate — translucent

options.label: B
options.text: Lamp shade — translucent; spectacle glass — opaque; plate — transparent

options.label: C
options.text: Lamp shade — translucent; spectacle glass — transparent; plate — opaque

options.label: D
options.text: Lamp shade — transparent; spectacle glass — translucent; plate — opaque

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. This directly tests the matching task from the Let us reflect section. A paper lamp shade allows some light through but not a clear view (translucent); spectacle glass is made to be seen through clearly (transparent); a ceramic plate blocks all light (opaque).
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can apply material property vocabulary to identify and justify the classification of familiar objects.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with disciplinary core ideas in the natural sciences, as well as in engineering, technology, and applications of science, which reflect the content that will be learned across subject areas in later Grades

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student has confused transparent and translucent — they may know the plate is opaque but have not distinguished between full and partial light transmission for the other two.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option shows the student has misclassified the paper lamp shade as opaque, possibly because paper in other contexts (e.g., thick cardboard) is opaque — a material-context confusion.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option reveals a more fundamental reversal: spectacle glass is placed as opaque and the plate as transparent, suggesting the student has not connected the terms to the light-transmission observations at all.
